title: Humidity readings above their greenhouse average
prompt:
A plant nursery logs humidity readings from sensors in several greenhouses. A failed sensor writes a NULL humidity.

Return every reading whose humidity is strictly greater than the average humidity of its own greenhouse. Compare each reading with its greenhouse, not with all greenhouses together.

- Columns: id, greenhouse, humidity
- Any row order is fine
- The average ignores NULL readings, and NULL readings are never returned
- A reading equal to the average is not returned
hints: The comparison value changes per row: it depends on the row's greenhouse.
A correlated subquery can refer to the outer row: (SELECT avg(...) FROM readings r2 WHERE r2.greenhouse = r.greenhouse).
WHERE r.humidity > (SELECT avg(r2.humidity) FROM readings r2 WHERE r2.greenhouse = r.greenhouse). avg() already skips NULLs, and NULL > x is never true.

exercise.schema: CREATE TABLE readings (id int PRIMARY KEY, greenhouse text NOT NULL, humidity numeric(5,1));
exercise.starter:
-- Readings above their greenhouse's average
SELECT id, greenhouse, humidity
FROM readings
WHERE humidity > (SELECT avg(humidity) FROM readings);
exercise.solution:
SELECT r.id, r.greenhouse, r.humidity
FROM readings r
WHERE r.humidity > (
  SELECT avg(r2.humidity)
  FROM readings r2
  WHERE r2.greenhouse = r.greenhouse
);

hiddenTests.name: reading equal to the average is excluded
NULL readings do not drag the average down
all-NULL and single-reading greenhouses
hiddenTests.seed: INSERT INTO readings VALUES (1, 'cactus', NULL), (2, 'cactus', NULL), (3, 'orchid', 88.0), (4, 'palm', 30.0), (5, 'palm', 31.5);

explanation: The subquery is correlated: it refers to r.greenhouse from the outer row, so each reading is compared with the average of its own greenhouse. avg() skips NULLs, so a failed sensor does not lower the average, and a NULL humidity is never greater than anything, so it is never returned. Strict > keeps readings that equal the average out. The trap is an uncorrelated subquery that compares every reading with one global average, or computing sum/count(*) by hand, which counts NULL rows.
notes: Postgres may run a correlated subquery once per outer row; an index on readings(greenhouse, humidity) makes each lookup cheap. A usually faster form computes all averages once, either with a CTE grouped by greenhouse and joined back, or with avg(humidity) OVER (PARTITION BY greenhouse) in a derived table. All three return the same rows.
followUps: Rewrite this with a window function and compare the plans.
Return readings more than one standard deviation above their greenhouse average.
